card.hook: Picture a wall of pink-tinted arches so big it fills your whole screen, with café tables at its feet making everyone look tiny. That's the Verona Arena, and it's hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Head for Piazza Bra, where the Arena is 62 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. For the classic view with more room, stand on the far side of the square and face the Arena.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the arches fill the frame without bending. If people or café tables crowd the foreground, try zoom 0.5x to catch more of the curve of the wall. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) is great for close-ups of the arches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level so the arches don't lean, then put the base of the wall on the lower line to squeeze in some of the square.
card.best_time: Go in the last twenty minutes before sunset, when the light is pleasant. Early morning works too, because the square is at its quietest then.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold your phone a little higher than usual. Switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, then turn so the Arena's arches sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is free to stand in, but going inside the Arena is ticketed. Photo rules can change during performances, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the arches fill the whole frame, then another with a café table tucked in the corner to show how big the Arena really is.
card.good_to_know: Verona Arena is a Roman amphitheatre and one of the best-preserved in the world, helped along by restoration work from the 16th century onwards. Experts still debate when it was built, but many point to the 1st century, which would make it older than the Colosseum in Rome. An opera festival has run here in summer since 1913, interrupted only by wars.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Piazza Bra, where the Arena is 62 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. For the classic view with more room, stand on the far side of the square and face the Arena.

card.hook: Picture a tiny courtyard where everyone is craning their neck at one little balcony, and you're trying to dodge about forty elbows. Good news: there's a sneakier spot with a much calmer view.
card.stand_here: Stand at La Casa di Giulietta, in the second-floor window of the embroidery shop next to the house entrance, and face down into the courtyard so the balcony is in view. If that's not an option, the courtyard floor works too: face the balcony above the bronze statue of Juliet and the ivy-covered walls.
card.zoom: In the crowded courtyard, use zoom 0.5x to fit the balcony, walls and statue into one frame. From the shop window, start at zoom 1x for the whole scene, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the balcony from above.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the balcony on one of the upper intersections, with the courtyard below as context.
card.best_time: Evening, when the house is closed. The view from the shop window may be quiet then, so you could have it almost to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, tap 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit higher than your face. Tilt it so the balcony sits over your shoulder, and take a few shots in case someone wanders into the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the courtyard can vary, so check the official site for current rules. To go up to the shop window you'd be expected to buy a personalised embroidery item, so confirm the shop still offers it.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the balcony with no stranger's head in it. Bonus points for patience, double bonus if you manage it with a smile.
card.good_to_know: Juliet's House is a small courtyard that people visit for its famous balcony. The courtyard and house may be ticketed through a single entrance at Teatro Nuovo in Piazzetta Navona, and the Via Cappello door is reportedly permanently closed. Give yourself a little extra time to line up your photo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at La Casa di Giulietta, in the second-floor window of the embroidery shop next to the house entrance, and face down into the courtyard so the balcony is in view. If that's not an option, the courtyard floor works too: face the balcony above the bronze statue of Juliet and the ivy-covered walls.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: this medieval castle has been quietly redesigned by a 20th-century architect, and you can spot his work in the doorways and staircases. Grab one wide shot first, then go hunting for stone.
card.stand_here: Stand at Ponte Castelvecchio, about 30 m south of the castle, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
card.zoom: Start at 1x with gridlines on, so the castle walls stay straight. If the whole building won't fit, tap 0.5x and keep the phone level. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the building, then slide it a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to old stone. Midday sun makes the shadows harsh.
card.selfie_here: Try the small raised stone ledge along Ponte Scaligero (the Castelvecchio bridge). Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and stand so the fortress fills the frame over your shoulder. Check the framing when you get there, as it's a good guess rather than a famous pose.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Adige riverbank, downstream of Ponte Scaligero, to shoot back toward the bridge and castle.
card.rules_and_safety: The raised walkways have no guardrails or handrails and the steps are narrow, so take care when posing near the edges. Check current visiting arrangements before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the castle walls line up with the vertical gridlines, then see if you can find a doorway or staircase that looks like a modern addition.
card.good_to_know: Castelvecchio is Verona's civic museum, inside the medieval castle it's named after. Architect Carlo Scarpa restored it between 1959 and 1973, keeping the castle's history visible and adding his own careful details. Inside you'll find sculpture, paintings, ancient weapons, ceramics, gold work and an equestrian statue of Cangrande I della Scala, which came from the Scaliger Tombs.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Ponte Castelvecchio, about 30 m south of the castle, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.

card.hook: Look up from the market stalls and you'll see a tall tower poking out over a row of painted houses. Piazza delle Erbe packs a lot into one view, so give yourself a minute to take it in.
card.stand_here: For the big view, go up the Torre dei Lamberti on the northern side of the square and look straight down at the stalls, the fountain and the rooftops. Staying at street level? Shoot along the length of the square with the tower rising above the frescoed houses.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square, the stalls and the rooftops into one shot. Switch to 1x for a natural look at the fountain and facades, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Madonna Verona statue, the frescoes or the River Adige in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain or the line of market stalls on one of the lines, then tap the brightest part of the sky and drag the slider to darker so the painted facades keep their colour.
card.best_time: One guide recommends sunrise or just after sunset for the view from the tower. After sunset, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the frescoed Case Mazzanti with the painted facades behind you, and the Torre dei Lamberti rises behind them. Or try the Madonna Verona fountain in the middle of the square. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the houses fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the south entrance of the piazza and shoot along its length with the Torre dei Lamberti in the frame, while you stand out in the square.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but the Torre dei Lamberti is ticketed, so check the official site for prices and hours before you go. Pickpockets are reported in busy squares, so keep an eye on your bag when it's crowded. Vendors, café seating and stalls can block the view, so be considerate and wait for a gap.
card.challenge: Find the white marble column with St Mark's Lion on the western side of the square and get it into a photo with the frescoed houses behind it.
card.good_to_know: Piazza delle Erbe is Verona's old market square, and it sits on the site of the town's Roman forum. The fountain was built in 1368, but the Madonna Verona statue on top is a Roman sculpture from 380 AD. The lion on the column is St Mark's Lion, the symbol of the Venetian Republic.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: For the big view, go up the Torre dei Lamberti on the northern side of the square and look straight down at the stalls, the fountain and the rooftops. Staying at street level? Shoot along the length of the square with the tower rising above the frescoed houses.

card.hook: Stand in the middle of Ponte Pietra and you're on a bridge that people have been crossing since 100 BC. Arches, river, rooftops and a hill, all in one frame, and you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ponte Pietra, mid-span, and face the old town and the Teatro Romano hill. The arches fill the foreground, with the rooftops and the hill behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the arches, river and rooftops all fit. Go to 0.5x for more of the arch up close, or try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the hill and rooftops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the line of the bridge along the lower third, so the river leads the eye up to the rooftops and the hill.
card.best_time: Sunset or golden hour suits it best. Early morning is the quieter option.
card.selfie_here: Cross the bridge heading away from the city centre and take the steps down to the Adige bank. One guide says it's usually quiet there. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the bridge is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of the whole arched bridge, ask someone to shoot from the west bank beneath the bridge deck, where the full row of arches fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The stone surface of Ponte Pietra can get slippery when it's wet, so watch your step. Be considerate of other people nearby.
card.challenge: Get the arches, the river, the rooftops and the hill into one frame, then check you've got all four before you move on.
card.good_to_know: Ponte Pietra, the "Stone Bridge", is the oldest bridge in Verona. It was completed in 100 BC, and the Via Postumia from Genoa to Aquileia once ran over it. Retreating German troops blew up four arches in World War II, and they were rebuilt in 1957 using the original materials.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ponte Pietra, mid-span, and face the old town and the Teatro Romano hill. The arches fill the foreground, with the rooftops and the hill behind them.

card.hook: Dante is standing in the middle of the square looking very serious, and he's the best free photo prop in Verona. Put him close to you, add a row of arches behind him, and you've got a tidy, good-looking shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza dei Signori, beside the Dante statue in the centre of the square. Face down the arcade so the statue is close to you and the line of arches leads away into the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit Dante and the palace facades into one wide shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the arches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines to keep the building edges straight, and tap the statue so it stays sharp. If the sky is bright, slide the picture a little darker so the facades don't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the time guides recommend, when low light falls across the square. It can get busy: the Christmas market fills it in December and opera season brings crowds in summer, so wait for a gap and take a few frames.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Dante statue in the middle of the square and turn so the arcades fill the background. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit higher so the statue and the stone frontage stay over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to wait under the Arco della Costa on the Piazza delle Erbe side while you walk through the arch and into the square, so the square opens up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep an eye on your bag in the busy squares, as you would anywhere. Events and markets can change how the square looks, so expect it to look different then.
card.challenge: Fit Dante, the line of arches and not a single stranger's elbow into one frame. Bonus points if you manage it in July.
card.good_to_know: Piazza dei Signori is a square in the middle of Verona, lined with arcaded palace facades. The Dante statue stands in the centre. Right next to it is the Arco della Costa, with a whale rib hanging from the arch.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza dei Signori, beside the Dante statue in the centre of the square. Face down the arcade so the statue is close to you and the line of arches leads away into the square.

card.hook: Torre dei Lamberti is 84 m of brick and stone, so the real challenge is getting it all on your screen. Your phone will think about it, then give you a lot of sky.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Torre dei Lamberti itself: the phone icon on the map is right at the foot of the tower. Face the tower and look straight up.
card.zoom: At the foot, use zoom 0.5x and tilt the phone up gently to fit the height in. If you can step back a few paces, switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the clock and the spot where the stone changes.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up one straight edge of the tower with a grid line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light shows off the texture of the brick and stone. Try not to shoot straight into the sun.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the steps at the tower's entrance, before you climb (you'll need your ticket first). Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and let the terracotta and peach brickwork rise behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone at the south entrance of Piazza delle Erbe and ask for a wide shot up the square with the tower in frame, while you stand in the piazza in view.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower is a visitor attraction, so any climb or entry may be ticketed or restricted. Check the official site before you go. The top platform has a metal mesh barrier that makes photos harder, so don't count on a clean shot up there.
card.challenge: Find the line where the old stonework turns to marble and get it in one zoomed shot together with the clock face.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1172. Lightning struck the top in May 1403, and repairs started in 1448 and took 16 years. The tower was extended then, which is why the newer sections use different materials, including marble. The big clock face was added in 1779, and the bell called Rengo was once rung to call people to arms or summon the city councils.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Torre dei Lamberti itself: the phone icon on the map is right at the foot of the tower. Face the tower and look straight up.

card.hook: Step out into Piazza Bra and you'll get it straight away. The name comes from 'braida', an old word for broad, and the whole Roman Arena sits at the end of all that open space.
card.stand_here: Head for Piazza Bra and stand on the far (east) side of the square. Turn around and face back across it toward the Arena.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole Arena across the square. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched view, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the Arena's arches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line. Then tap the Arena's stone and slide the brightness down a little so the warm stone keeps its colour and the sky stays deep blue.
card.best_time: Aim for the last twenty minutes before sunset, when the stone glows warm. Blue hour just afterwards is lovely too. Switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Grab an outdoor table at one of the cafés lining Piazza Bra, with the Arena rising behind you. Hold your front camera at arm's length (try 0.5x if your phone offers it) and keep the Arena over your shoulder so it blurs softly behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the square facing the Arena while you pose with the Arena behind you, ideally in the last twenty minutes before sunset.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos in the square are generally fine, but drones or commercial shoots may need permits. Selfie sticks are banned inside the Arena itself, and opera and concert nights can mean big crowds and photo restrictions, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get the whole Arena in one shot with the horizon on the lower gridline, plus one stranger strolling through for scale.
card.good_to_know: The Arena was built in the 1st century AD and defined the northern edge of what became the square. The Liston, the paved promenade along the edge, was begun in 1770, and Goethe wrote about the crowds walking here. For a second shot, walk to the Portoni della Bra, a double-arched gate with arches from the late 14th and mid-15th centuries and a clock added in 1871.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Piazza Bra and stand on the far (east) side of the square. Turn around and face back across it toward the Arena.

card.hook: Most bridges just get you across the river. This one looks like a castle wall that wandered off and decided to stand in the Adige, with red brick above, white marble below and a fortress right behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lungadige Cangrande, the riverbank on the castle side, downstream (east) of the bridge. The bridge lies to the south of you, so face south and step back until the whole span and the castle fit in one frame.
card.zoom: If the riverbank is narrow and you can't step back far enough, use zoom 0.5x to squeeze the bridge and castle together. Where there's room, zoom 1x looks more natural, and zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) gets you in close on the arches and brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brickwork, then drag the slider down so it's a little darker, which stops the sky washing out and keeps the brick nicely red.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light on the brick. Guides disagree on the single best moment, so check the light on the day. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep still.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto the Ponte Scaligero walkway to mid-span, stand beside a gap in the crenellated parapet and face back toward Castelvecchio. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it) and hold it so the battlements frame you and the fortress sits over your shoulder. For a second option, stand on the riverside path next to the bridge with the arches behind you, so the red brick stays easy to read.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand on the riverbank a few paces back from the bridge, while you pose nearer to it, so the full arched span and Castelvecchio fill the photo.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is a free pedestrian crossing and the riverbank is a public street, so keep an eye out for people walking into the edge of your shot.
card.challenge: Take the same shot from the riverbank and from the bridge, then see if friends can believe they're the same place.
card.good_to_know: The bridge is about 120 m long, and its main arch spans 48.70 m, which was the largest bridge arch in the world when it was built, most likely in 1354-1356 for Cangrande II della Scala. Retreating German troops destroyed it on 24 April 1945. Architect Libero Cecchini rebuilt it between 1949 and 1951.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lungadige Cangrande, the riverbank on the castle side, downstream (east) of the bridge. The bridge lies to the south of you, so face south and step back until the whole span and the castle fit in one frame.

card.hook: Count the windows: twelve little arches stacked in two neat rows above two big ones, all in pale stone. It's like a Roman building that was drawn with a ruler, and it's the main reason this gate is so easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand on Corso Cavour, on the street side facing the gate's façade. From here you see the one surviving face of the Roman gate head-on, with both arches and the windows above.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole façade. If the street is too tight to get the top windows in, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved capitals and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up the centre pillar between the arches with the middle vertical line, and hold your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet, because the area gets busy at midday. Repair work has been reported on the gate, so scaffolding or covers might block part of the view and you may need to adjust your framing.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the archway opening on the Corso Porta Borsari side, with the gate's stonework behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the arch fits in, and keep the stonework over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Corso Porta Borsari, a few steps back from the arches, so the full façade and the upper windows fit in the frame with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy pedestrian street, so step aside after your shots to keep people moving. Repair work has been reported, so check what you can see before you go.
card.challenge: Take one perfectly straight-on shot with the centre pillar sitting right on the grid line, then try to prove all twelve windows are there.
card.good_to_know: Porta Borsari dates to the 1st century AD, and an inscription records a rebuild in 265 AD. The Via Postumia, a Roman road, ran through it. The name comes from the guard soldiers who were paid the dazio (bursarii), and the Romans themselves called it Porta Iovia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Corso Cavour, on the street side facing the gate's façade. From here you see the one surviving face of the Roman gate head-on, with both arches and the windows above.

card.hook: You've huffed your way up past the cypresses, and then the whole of Verona opens up below you, rooftops, bell towers and all. Not bad for a few minutes of climbing.
card.stand_here: Stand on the upper belvedere of Giardino Giusti, at the top of the garden after the climb past the cypresses. It's about 2 minutes on foot from the palazzo in a straight line, though the climb takes a little longer. Face out over the city so the dark cypresses frame the view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the big rooftop view. Tap 2x to pick out the bell towers (higher zooms depend on your phone). Go to 0.5x in the cypress alley and at the maze.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the bright city and drag the brightness down a touch so the sky and rooftops keep their colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is a good bet, when the light over the city is softer and warmer. Check the official site for opening times.
card.selfie_here: Take it from the raised belvedere above the stone mask, the garden's highest point, so the garden and Verona's rooftops fit around you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more in, and keep the view over your shoulder. Or step into the long cypress lane just past the main gate, where the trees frame you on both sides.
card.ask_someone: Stand in the courtyard just inside the main gate, facing the six-arched portico and the cypress avenue beyond, and ask the visitor to stand in the avenue.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is allowed everywhere in the garden, but organised or professional shoots may need permission, so check the garden's rules first. Paths are paved but sometimes uneven, so wear closed shoes.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the cypresses make a dark frame on both sides, and get Verona's rooftops sitting neatly in the gap.
card.good_to_know: The garden was laid out from 1580 and is often called one of the finest Italian gardens. The Giusti family were allowed to add 'del Giardino' to their surname because the garden mattered so much. A severe storm in 2020 killed many trees, including the 600-year-old Goethe cypress, so don't look for it near the entrance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the upper belvedere of Giardino Giusti, at the top of the garden after the climb past the cypresses. It's about 2 minutes on foot from the palazzo in a straight line, though the climb takes a little longer. Face out over the city so the dark cypresses frame the view.

card.hook: Look down at the porch before you look up: its portico rests on the backs of two stone griffins. Verona Cathedral's front is packed with carved detail, so your camera roll will thank you.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Duomo, in front of the west facade, and face the cathedral. From there the cathedral is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole front. If the square is crowded and you can't step back, try 0.5x. Then go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the porch carvings, the griffins and the bronze angel statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the central porch up with the middle of the frame and keep the phone level, then tap the stonework and drag the slider slightly darker so the pale facade and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing front best, when it catches warmer, lower light. Early morning is usually quieter if you want the square without crowds.
card.selfie_here: Stand in Piazza Duomo with the cathedral's front behind you, near the bronze angel statue, and use the front camera (try 0.5x to fit more in). For a second selfie, stand mid-span on Ponte Pietra with the bell tower behind you across the river. One guide recommends the bridge for sunset shots.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far side of the square facing the cathedral, while you stand in front of the whole facade.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a place of worship, so check the official site for visiting times and any dress code. Photos inside are allowed without flash. Keep an eye on your bag in the busy squares.
card.challenge: Find Roland and Oliver in the walls either side of the doorway, then get both of them into one photo.
card.good_to_know: An earthquake in 1117 destroyed two earlier churches on this spot, and the new cathedral was consecrated in 1187. The porch sculpture is by the twelfth-century sculptor Nicholaus. The bell tower was begun in the 16th century by Michele Sanmicheli and never finished.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Duomo, in front of the west facade, and face the cathedral. From there the cathedral is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot.

card.hook: Picture the Adige curling through Verona like a lazy green ribbon, with a Roman bridge right under your feet and bell towers poking out of the rooftops. That's the view from up here, and yes, it's the postcard one.
card.stand_here: Stand on Piazzale Castel San Pietro, the open terrace in front of the old barracks on the hilltop, and face out over the historic centre. The castle is just to the north-west, so step a little way along the terrace and turn that way when you want it in the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole panorama, then 1x for a natural view of the rooftops. Then zoom in to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Ponte Pietra, a bell tower, or the Arena far off on a clear day.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and set the river bend along one of the lines, so the curve leads the eye into the city with Ponte Pietra below as your anchor.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into golden hour is the sweet spot, and it's a favourite for sunset. Stay on into blue hour and switch on night mode once it gets dusky. It can get crowded at busy times, so arrive early for a good spot.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the wall halfway down the ramp, to the left of the main viewing area at the top. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the city spread out over your shoulder, or hand your phone to a friend to shoot you against the wall.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Ponte Pietra and ask a passer-by to frame you with the castle hill rising up behind the bridge.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and videos for personal use are fine, but commercial photography may need prior authorization. Wear sensible shoes, because the ground can be uneven and slippery in places.
card.challenge: On a clear day, see if you can spot the Arena in the distance and get it into a shot with a bell tower beside it.
card.good_to_know: The terrace is free to enter, but the castle building isn't open to visitors, so treat it as a backdrop. To get up here, climb the Scalinata S. Pietro from Ponte Pietra or take the funicular (check the official site for times and tickets). For a calmer angle, look for the brick wall or ramp near the restaurant at the top. It isn't marked on the map, so keep your eyes open.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Piazzale Castel San Pietro, the open terrace in front of the old barracks on the hilltop, and face out over the historic centre. The castle is just to the north-west, so step a little way along the terrace and turn that way when you want it in the shot.

card.hook: Most people queue up at the front of this 2,000-year-old arch for the classic shot. You're going round the back, where the river, a little park and the bridge make a much calmer picture.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on the river side of the Arco dei Gavi, in the small square beside Castelvecchio. Face the arch, with the Adige, the park and the bridge behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the arch, river and bridge all fit together. If the park and riverbank feel squashed, try 0.5x. Use 2x to get close to the columns and stonework without stepping toward the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the arch on one side and let the river and bridge fill the other, then tap the arch and slide it a touch darker so the pale stone keeps its detail against bright sky or water.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset is your best bet, when the stone looks warmer and the riverside feels calmer.
card.selfie_here: Try the grassy riverside strip next to the arch, facing back toward it so the castle bridge is in the frame. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low, so the arch sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the open square side in front of the arch, so the full opening and its columns fit, while you pose in front of the arch.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photography at the arch is generally allowed. It's right beside a busy street, so watch the traffic and the people walking past when you step back. If you shoot from the bridge, the walkways are narrow with no guardrails.
card.challenge: Take the same arch twice, once from the postcard front and once from the river side, then see which one your friends like more.
card.good_to_know: The arch dates from the first half of the 1st century AD and was built for the Gavia family, a noble line with roots in Verona. It's a rare example of a monumental arch paid for privately. French engineers took it apart in 1805, and it was rebuilt from the original stones and finished in 1932.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on the river side of the Arco dei Gavi, in the small square beside Castelvecchio. Face the arch, with the Adige, the park and the bridge behind it.

card.hook: Look up. High above Via Arche Scaligere, stone lords in full armour sit on their horses on top of Gothic canopies, and most people walk past while looking at their phones.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on Via Arche Scaligere at the corner by the Piazza dei Signori exit, right by the iron grilles. Face the grilles so the tombs and the church wall of Santa Maria Antica fill your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the grilles, the tombs and the church wall in one shot. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single horseman or a carved canopy.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stone of the tomb, not the bars, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the carving keeps its detail against the black ironwork.
card.best_time: One photography guide says late afternoon gives warmer light and deeper shadows. Another says late morning is more balanced, so pick the look you like.
card.selfie_here: Try the iron grille on the street side of the enclosure, with the tombs behind you. Use the front camera, and zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, so the tombs sit over your shoulder. They'll be more background than centre stage, but the grille makes a nice frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The tomb enclosure is closed to visitors, so you look in through the grilles from the street. Access may change, so check current information locally before you go.
card.challenge: Spot the little stair pattern worked into the ironwork, then get it in the foreground with a horseman sharp behind it.
card.good_to_know: These are five Gothic tombs for the Scaliger (Della Scala) family, who ruled Verona from the 13th to the late 14th century. The stair motif in the ironwork is a nod to the family name, which means 'of the stairs'. Cangrande I's tomb was the first built, over a doorway in the church wall, and the horseman on it is a copy, because the original is in the Castelvecchio museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on Via Arche Scaligere at the corner by the Piazza dei Signori exit, right by the iron grilles. Face the grilles so the tombs and the church wall of Santa Maria Antica fill your screen.

card.hook: Imagine a whole hillside of ancient stone seats rising straight up from the river, with a bridge right in front of it to stand on. That's Verona's Roman Theatre from Ponte Pietra, and it's about as good as a free view gets.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ponte Pietra, either mid-bridge or at the old-town end, and face east to south-east toward the theatre. From the old-town end, the theatre is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the theatre, the Santo Stefano church and the curve of the river all fit in. Then try 2x or more to pick out the curved rows of seats. If you're down on the riverbank steps, zoom 0.5x gets the whole hillside from a low angle.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hillside, then drag the brightness slider down a little if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Several guides suggest sunset for the light on the river. One guide prefers the Castel San Pietro terrace at sunrise for a view from above.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the stage area of the Roman Theatre, in front of the ancient stonework with the stage behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and try 0.5x so the stonework fills the space over your shoulder. One guide says the stage looks dramatic in daylight, or at night when it's lit.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the embankment on the Old Town side of the Adige, near Ponte Pietra, and shoot back toward the theatre's main facade, with you posing in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Ponte Pietra and the riverbank are open public spaces, but the theatre's upper terraces and museum are ticketed, so check the official site before you go. Scaffolding and summer seating were reported over the seating recently, so some steps may be hidden.
card.challenge: Wait for someone to stroll across the bridge, then catch them as a tiny figure with the whole theatre hillside behind them.
card.good_to_know: The theatre dates from the late 1st century BC, and what you see today was uncovered from around 1830. The church of S. Siro was built over part of the seating in the 10th century and restored in the 14th. Walls were built along the Adige here in Roman times to guard against floods, so the river and theatre have long belonged together.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ponte Pietra, either mid-bridge or at the old-town end, and face east to south-east toward the theatre. From the old-town end, the theatre is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east.

card.hook: Picture a rose-coloured church front across a square, café tables at the edges and a huge carved stone wheel staring back at you. That's San Zeno, and it makes the facade easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza San Zeno, right in front of the west facade. The basilica is to the north-east of you, so face it head-on with the bell tower beside it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the straight-on view of the facade and bell tower. If you step in close, try 0.5x to fit the whole front in. Then go to 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the rose window and the bronze portal panels.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the facade up with the middle vertical line and keep your phone level so the front doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing facade best. Earlier in the day the square tends to be calmer, so it's easier to get a clear view.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the basilica's own front steps, so the church stands right behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and a travel guide says early morning light is best here.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in the piazza, across from the facade, and shoot head-on so the whole front of the church fits in, while you pose on the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, photos are generally allowed without flash, but check the official site before you go. The basilica is a place of worship and may charge for entry.
card.challenge: Find the big round rose window, the "Wheel of Fortune", and zoom in until it fills your screen. Then pull back and see if you can fit the bell tower in too.
card.good_to_know: San Zeno is a Romanesque church and is considered a masterpiece of medieval architecture. It stands on a site with at least five earlier religious buildings, going back to a church over the tomb of Saint Zeno, who died between 372 and 380. The rebuilding began around the end of the 11th century, the 1117 earthquake interrupted it, and by about 1138 much of the present church was finished. The rose window was carved by Brioloto de Balneo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza San Zeno, right in front of the west facade. The basilica is to the north-east of you, so face it head-on with the bell tower beside it.

card.hook: Most grand churches wear marble. Sant'Anastasia, Verona's biggest and grandest, never finished its front, so you get warm bare red brick and one show-off Gothic doorway. It looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Sant'Anastasia, on the western side of the square, and face the church front straight on. The little Church of San Giorgetto and the Castelbarco tomb sit beside the doorway, so they'll slip into your shot too.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and a slice of square. Switch to 1x for a calmer look with less stretching at the edges. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to home in on the doorway and the brick.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the edges of the facade up with them, and hold your phone upright so the building doesn't lean backwards.
card.best_time: Go early, when the square is usually quieter. Soft, even light is kind to the brick, so skip the harsh midday glare if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try the Ark of Castelbarco, under the passageway arch on the church's left side, with the church front behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more in. Ponte Pietra is a second option: face the river with the church's bell tower behind you. Check both on site.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across the square so the whole front fits, while you stand in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is closed at some times for services, so shoot the outside first and go in only if it's open. Inside, photos are fine without flash, and please respect any service going on.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then find the brick that's the warmest red and fill the whole frame with it. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Dominican friars were given the land in 1260 and building began in 1290. It dragged on for generations, and the church was consecrated on 22 October 1471. It stands at the end of the decumanus maximus, the main street of Roman Verona, close to the bend of the Adige river by Ponte Pietra.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Sant'Anastasia, on the western side of the square, and face the church front straight on. The little Church of San Giorgetto and the Castelbarco tomb sit beside the doorway, so they'll slip into your shot too.

card.hook: Let's be honest: from up on the hill, San Fermo might be a tiny speck in a big, beautiful scene, or hide completely. Take the wide shot first and treat spotting the church as a bonus game.
card.stand_here: Stand on Castel San Pietro, the hillside terrace above the Adige, reached on foot from the north end of Ponte Pietra. The church is about 1 km to the south, so face south over the old town, with Ponte Pietra, the cathedral and the river in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole panorama. If you can pick out the church, go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a second shot, and use 0.5x if you want the whole bend of the river. Want the church as the star? Ponte Navi gives a river-side view of it with its tall bell tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the river on a lower line, and let the rooftops fill the middle with sky above.
card.best_time: Sunrise and golden hour are your best bets.
card.selfie_here: Try the main terrace of Castel San Pietro, at the top of the climb: use the front camera, turn your back to the city and hold the phone a bit out, or switch to 0.5x to fit more in. Don't expect San Fermo right behind you, because it shows up only in the distant view.
card.ask_someone: For a proper church photo, ask someone to stand on Stradone San Fermo, across from the main portal, while you pose near the portal so the facade fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace is reached on foot by steps, so wear comfortable shoes. The church is a place of worship and may have visiting rules and fees, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you spot the church's pointy pinnacles on the skyline and zoom in on them without losing the river?
card.good_to_know: San Fermo Maggiore is a Romanesque and Gothic church dedicated to Saints Firmus and Rusticus, two brothers remembered as local martyrs from the 3rd century. A church is thought to have stood here since the 8th century, and the Benedictines added an upper storey and a bell tower by the 11th. The campanile was only finished in the 13th century. Inside you'll find medieval frescos and the Brenzoni Monument, with Pisanello's Annunciation fresco above it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Castel San Pietro, the hillside terrace above the Adige, reached on foot from the north end of Ponte Pietra. The church is about 1 km to the south, so face south over the old town, with Ponte Pietra, the cathedral and the river in front of you.
